articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Recreation Department are facing legal action with plaintiffs seeking to require the City to conduct and implement noise reduction measures at the Linda Beach pickleball courts. A trial date has been set for May 1. The lawsuit deals with the City’s decision to create permanent pickleball courts at the Linda Beach play area without doing any review under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), especially as it pertains to noise impact on residents with homes as close as 30 feet away. Adopted on September 5, 2023, Piedmont City Council approved the dedication and restriping of two Linda Beach Tennis Courts into four courts exclusively for pickleball use. The suit seeks to require the City to implement noise mitigation measures such as noise baffles, noise reducing equipment, possible restriction of hours, and considering alternative locations so that pickleball play can be distributed throughout the city. Neighbors of the area first approached attorney Richard Drury of Lozeau Drury LLP on September 22, 2023, taking issue with the City’s hasty decision. According to the opening trial brief, the sound generated by pickleball is four times louder than that generated by the felt-covered balls used in tennis, with a higher pitch and impulsive quality. This is potentially compounded by the court’s location in a valley, roughly 50 feet below

articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) was approved by the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) for a Grants for Arts Projects award of $20,000 last month. Many friends of the choir have been extending their congratulations to PEBCC and their inspiring Artistic Director Eric Tuan. The grant will go to support Echoes of Eureka, a mostly textless choral opera focused on the experiences of Chinese citizens during the Expulsion Acts in the 19th century. The opera, composed by Tuan, will premiere as a part of PEBCC’s Making History Concert this spring on April 12. It will also be performed at a music festival in Eureka in early May. Established by Congress in 1965, the NEA is an independent federal agency and one of the largest funders of the arts and arts education in communities nationwide. “Getting a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts is always a great moment,” said Bob Geary, founding Artistic Director of the choir. “It’s one of the most important things that a composer and an artist can do is to help us experience events or events that are happening, or have happened, that have been covered up or ignored, that have some deeper implications for who we are as human beings and citizens. “The award represents the view, nationally, of the quality of the Piedmont choirs.” The grant-writing process that led to the award was over 18 months in the making and is one of the most sizable grants that the organization has received. “It’s an important story that needs to be told. And we’re very honored to be able to bring this work to life through the support and the recognition by our peers at the national level at the NEA,” said Keri Butkevich, former Executive Director of the choir. The Artist: Eric Tuan Tuan is currently serving his sixth season as the Artistic Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, as well as Eric Tuan at his studio office at PEBCC

LETTERS - MAIN More on the problem of 210 Howard Editor: Continuing my discussion of the of 210 Howard Avenue SB 9/ Division 17.54 project, I learned the owner/developer and the City had several meetings and discussions prior to the SB 9/Division 17.54 application submittal, where the owner/developer presented pre-application conceptual dimensioned site plan(s). Typically, at such meetings, Planning Staff will advise a developer that they should make a project application after they got the design correct in terms of safety and health impacts, correct site layouts, proper fire exiting, paths of travel, code compliance, etc. Here, Staff may have also advised the owner/developer that the project would require obtaining neighbors’ permission to access or build on their properties because of the project’s retaining walls on each common property line. Afterwards, the owner/developer submitted their application, perhaps thinking that the neighbors were going to say: “I will gladly grant you permission to come onto my property so that you can construct your out of scale project which may prove to be unsafe, dangerous and might harm my property and house”. Frankly, I don’t understand how this project got so far. This is costing the City money and costing the staff time. This is not right. At 210 Howard, there are many health and safety issues in the current application that would cause a non SB 9/Division 17.54 project to be denied outright, such as code compliance, exiting, means of egress, retaining walls, driveway/walkway, exterior stair, fire issues and the City’s own Division 17.54 “path of travel” provision, etc. On 1/10/2025, the City issued a “Notice of Incompleteness” that accepted the developer’s plans and documents as is, and indicated that certain information needed to be included in the submitted materials in order for City staff to deem the application complete. Several minor clarifications were called out regarding the all-important site plan. Nowhere in this Notice, I believe, is there mention of the need to fix, revise or redesign project site elements that are required to meet standard health and safety standards. Per SB 9/ Division 17.54, the City, within 60 days after deeming the application is complete, will issue an approval or denial of the application based on specific standards. articles.text: Editor: The disruption of the Federal government that is taking place under the new presidential administration is utilizing conservative policy suggestions for the executive branch taken from Mandate for Leadership, a nearly 900-page book published by The Heritage Foundation as part of its Project 2025 effort. The chapter on the Department of Education calls for major changes, most notably: 1) the breakup of the Department of Education with the transfer of most of its programs to other Federal agencies; and 2) providing the option for every parent “to direct his or her child’s share of education funding through an education savings account, funded overwhelming by state and local taxpayers, which would empower parents to choose a set of education options that meet their child’s unique needs.” I spoke to the Piedmont School Board at its February 12 meeting regarding the Project 2025 proposals and the fact that they could have a dramatic impact on public education, most notably in causing decreased enrollment and attendant funding because of the non-public school options that would become economically attractive to Piedmont families with school age children. I made four suggestions to the Board members which were summarized in an email I sent to them the next day and are copied below: 1. If you have not done so already, familiarize yourself with the chapter on the Department of Education from the Project 2025 book. 2. Consider how you will deal with the elimination of the Department of Education (DOE) if/when it happens. 3. Be transparent with the school and general community about the status of this issue and deliberations you may have on it. 4. Consider taking an advocacy role if you think the elimination of the DOE is problematic by any of a number of means, e.g, engaging the community in protest activities, collaborating with other school districts, etc. A few of the plans in this chapter have already been implemented including the reduction of the indirect (overhead) cost rate for research performed at universities which can have a crippling effect on their research efforts and the order by the Trump administration for colleges and K-12 schools to abolish diversity, education, and inclusion (DEI) or to risk funding cuts. Though my children are well beyond school age, I think that policies that negatively impact the funding and quality of our schools are important to our entire community and encourage you to think about how we can deal with them. articles.text: The City of Piedmont invites residents to complete a brief online survey about their experiences with parking in Piedmont’s Civic Center. Looking ahead to the completion of construction of the new community pool and the city’s 911 dispatch center, the City is conducting a review of public parking on Bonita, Hillside, Highland, Magnolia, and Vista Avenues. When these projects are complete, some parking spaces that had been removed to accommodate construction will become available again. At the same time, the expanded pool facility is expected to draw more visitors to the area. Understanding how community members experience trips to the Civic Center now will provide important context to inform any changes proposed for the future. The short, 9-question survey asks community members to share: • How they generally get to the Civic Center (drive, walk, bicycle) • How long they tend to stay • How easy or difficult it is generally to find parking • How they feel about the current balance of time-limited parking spaces (30 minute, 2 hour) The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ParkingSurvey and will be open through Wednesday, March 12. This comprehensive review follows several years of disruption to historical parking distribution in the Civic Center area, beginning with the construction of the new STEAM building and theater on the Piedmont High School campus, when “Permit A” restrictions were added to existing parking spaces along Magnolia. An additional 57 spaces were lost in 2023 when construction began on the new community pool. Further spaces were removed or redesignated in summer 2024 to accommodate construction on the Police Department’s new 9-1-1 dispatch center. A discussion of parking reconfiguration options in the Civic Center is tentatively scheduled for the March 17 City Council meeting. City staff will present a scenario that maximizes the number of available parking spaces. The Council will provide preliminary guidance to staff for discussion and action later this spring. Survey responses, as well as direct outreach to stakeholders in the area, will provide data to inform this discussion.

articles.text: The Superior Court of Alameda County is seeking residents to serve on the Alameda County Civil Grand Jury. The jury’s primary responsibility is to examine and report on the operations of local government agencies and to investigate citizen complaints, acting as the public’s watchdog. Working as an arm of the Superior Court, the Civil Grand Jury is comprised of 19 citizens authorized to investigate local government to ensure that public agencies are working in the best interests of the public. Its independence gives the Grand Jury a unique role in securing local government accountability and in examining allegations of misconduct. Jury members work to investigate citizen complaints and examine the operations of local government agencies across Alameda County. This work involves reading and analyzing investigative materials, questioning witnesses and writing reports. Serving on the Grand Jury can be a rewarding experience, but also a significant commitment – the jury meets twice a week (Wednesday and Thursday mornings) for a year. Most jurors devote additional time beyond this to their service. Grand jurors are paid $15/day plus mileage and/or public transportation reimbursement. Several Piedmont residents have served on the Grand Jury. Applications for the 2025-2026 term (starting July 1) are due by April 15. To apply, visit the Alameda County Grand Jury website at https://grandjury.acgov.org/ join-us/.

B. Curtis. As an Actor, producer, real estate developer, promoter, hotelier, benefactor, and murder suspect, Curtis reached the highs of celebrity and fame as well as the lows of failure, illness, and a faltering career. Richard Schwartz’s book The Man Who Lit Lady Liberty rescues his story from the dusty archives of forgotten history and reexamines an actor whose creativity and cultural influence still resonate today. “In this outstanding new biography of that remarkable immigrant thespian M.B. Curtis, Richard Schwartz gives readers a lost episode in the story of the Statue of Liberty and her torch ― that it was Curtis himself who helped pay for Miss Liberty’s first electric lighting bills in November 1886. This is just one of the many absorbing episodes in this biography of one of the most talented character actors of his time,” said Barry Moreno, Historian and author at the Bob Hope Memorial Library at Ellis Island. Richard Schwartz is a historian and the author of Eccentrics, Heroes, and Cutthroats of Old Berkeley, Earthquake Exodus, 1906, Berkeley 1900, and The Circle of Stones. articles.text: School districts in California must report a mid-year update of their Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP) before February 28, as required by Senate Bill 114. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich gave the update during the February 12 school board meeting. Of note, Dolowich reported on the progress updating the English Language Arts (ELA) curriculum for elementary students and improved teacher satisfaction with Staff “Professional Development” days. The district is currently in the first year of this three-year LCAP with the following goals prioritized. Goal #1: Creating an Environment to Thrive Goal #2: Investing in Outstanding Academics Goal #3: Partnering Beyond the Classroom Goal #4: Building for Operational Excellence Within Goal #2, Dolowich gave a timeline of the work on the adoption of new elementary level ELA curriculum. The process of switching to either “Benchmark Advance” or “Fishtank Learning” options began in the fall. PUSD, like many other districts, is switching from the curriculum developed by Lucy Calkins, which is now considered outdated. The new curriculum at the three elementary schools will be pilot programs this year. Teachers involved and admin plan to make a recommendation of action by May 7, and plan to seek board approval on May 28. “Previously, the board adopted ‘from phonics to reading [and spellography for]’ K-3,” said Dolowich. “‘Fishtank’ would keep that in place and it would just add a knowledge base, it’s complementary, whereas ‘Benchmark [Advance]’ is comprehensive,” he explained. Dolowich reported a focus on making the district-wide professional development sessions more meaningful. He showed data that this year’s pro-development, with six workshops instead of a keynote speaker, resulted in teachers rating the workdays as helpful in developing a sense of community. “I’m delighted to see the rightward shift in professional development scores,” said Board Vice President Ruchi Medhekar. “I think it’s a testament of how much attention and care you all have taken to put that together.” Dolowich mentioned attendance of the optional, professional development days was paltry when he first arrived in the district, with around 80% of teachers not attending. “The real goal is attendance. What we have seen is more people attending in the last two years,” he said. Board members, student and elected, expressed some apprehension over the results of a portion of the CA Healthy Kids survey which measured student stress. Last year’s data was organized based on how many AP and Honors classes students are taking. PHS student representative to the board Mira Sachs noted that she and her peers took this year’s Healthy Kids survey that same day. “I think a lot of times, they are pretty long tests and ‘I just randomly clicked,’ is sometimes what people say, probably a majority of people take it serious though,” Sachs noted. Board member Max Roman pointed out that language around the words “anxiety” and “worry” in the high school surveys was worth examining. “Some anxiety, I would argue, is good and it gets you to achieve. Do you feel worried? To me it’s a tricky question.” said Roman. Dolowich acknowledged the limitations of surveys and the need for anecdotal feedback and first hand observations to decipher student mental health. The recording of the February 12 school board meeting is available at Piedmont.granicus.com/ player/clip/3024?view_id=9&redirect=true
articles.title: Dolowich highlights district activity in LCAP report

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School (PMS) Parents Club is now selling tickets for a PMS fundraiser on Thursday, March 27, “Kickin’ It Old Skool.” This is the school’s biggest fundraiser and will take place at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Party-goers will eat, drink, and dance the night away to favorite music from the 80’s and 90’s. The Kickin’ it Old Skool event, formerly known as “March Mingle,” will feature a live auction with special items including a Lake Tahoe vacation rental, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, and sporting event tickets. Old school sneakers like Vans and Keds are recommended. There will also be a raffle and surprises that can be described as “totally radical.” Don’t miss the rare opportunity to relive memories of junior high school days and the culture unique to the era. The event will be co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several Parent Parties, including a Pub Quiz night and Intro to Poker. The PMS Parents Club hopes the parents parties will help raise funds to support school programs. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27, knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Funds will support: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking out a few more Parent Sponsors. The district is currently in the first year of this three-year LCAP with the following goals prioritized. Goal #1: Creating an Environment to Thrive Goal #2: Investing in Outstanding Academics Goal #3: Partnering Beyond the Classroom Goal #4: Building for Operational Excellence Within Goal #2, Dolowich gave a timeline of the work on the adoption of new elementary level ELA curriculum. The process of switching to either “Benchmark Advance” or “Fishtank Learning” options began in the fall. PUSD, like many other districts, is switching from the curriculum developed by Lucy Calkins, which is now considered outdated. The new curriculum at the three elementary schools will be pilot programs this year. Teachers involved and admin plan to make a recommendation of action by May 7, and plan to seek board approval on May 28. “Previously, the board adopted ‘from phonics to reading [and spellography for]’ K-3,” said Dolowich. “‘Fishtank’ would keep that in place and it would just add a knowledge base, it’s complementary, whereas ‘Benchmark [Advance]’ is comprehensive,” he explained. What we have seen is more people attending in the last two years,” he said. Board members, student and elected, expressed some apprehension over the results of a portion of the CA Healthy Kids survey which measured student stress. Last year’s data was organized based on how many AP and Honors classes students are taking. PHS student representative to the board Mira Sachs noted that she and her peers took this year’s Healthy Kids survey that same day. “I think a lot of times, they are pretty long tests and ‘I just randomly clicked,’ is sometimes what people say, probably a majority of people take it serious though,” Sachs noted. Board member Max Roman pointed out that language around the words “anxiety” and “worry” in the high school surveys was worth examining. “Some anxiety, I would argue, is good and it gets you to achieve. Do you feel worried? To me it’s a tricky question.” said Roman. Dolowich acknowledged the limitations of surveys and the need for anecdotal feedback and first hand observations to decipher student mental health. articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council is hard at work inventing adventures for its annual Cub Scout Day Camp. Returning to Dracena Park the week after school lets out for the summer, Piedmont Cub Scouts and all youth (1st to 5th graders) will put their creativity to the test with Day Camp’s theme “Invention Convention.” During Day Camp on June 9-13 Piedmont Council will offer a wide range of daily activities including Scout skills, which showcases the Scouting program, sports and games, which get campers running about and staying active, arts and crafts, which challenges creativity, and more. While Day Camp always has new activities, the week will end with a traditional visit by the Piedmont Fire Department to host the traditional egg drop from its 80-foot extension ladder. Camper parents and family are invited to join for a picnic in the park while they watch the eggs fall. Day Camp is planned by a collaborative team of youth from the Council’s five Scout troops and the Community Service crew. The staff leadership team guides campers through all the fun activities they’ve prepared. Returning to oversee Day Camp is the Erin Ashton, in tandem with youth leaders Theo Ferguson and Kajsa Benson. The Council is preparing for a program filled with adventure in Dracena Park, “We’re always excited for Day Camp,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “It brings our youth, both young and old, together for an experience they rarely get. They sing songs, make new friends, work together, and have fun outdoors.” Interested youth can register for Day Camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Community Pass catalog (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). Registration will stay open until the camp is full. Youth interested in joining Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing, or Exploring are encouraged to contact the Piedmont Scout council for more information at 510-844-4752 or contact@piedmontbsa.org. Additionally, you can visit their website at www. piedmontbsa.org, or visit them at the Piedmont Scout Office at 10 Highland Way in Piedmont. The Scout summer day camp opens with a traditional flag ceremony. Staff members and campers hop to it in one of Day Camp’s end of day activities.

articles.text: Register now for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir summer music camp and sing under the stars with your friends. PEBCC’s popular camp program for singers ages 7-11, Camp Joyful Voices, has added a second week by popular demand and spaces are filling quickly. Designed for young singers, this weeklong sleepaway camp is the perfect opportunity for your child to build confidence, deepen musical skills, and make new friends. With supportive staff and skilled counselors, your singer is sure to make lifelong memories and friendships while nurturing their love for singing. If your kid is always singing in the car and around the house, this is the perfect summer camp for them! Singing in a choir not only helps kids experience the joy and power of making music; it also teaches them teamwork, communication, empathy, and how to be a part of something larger than themselves. Our campers rehearse around 2 to 4 hours a day, grouped into ensembles by age and experience level. All campers participate in small voice classes with vocal experts. Children are encouraged to sing at the lake, on hikes, and around the campfire. Campers can go kayaking and boating, explore the creek bed, make friendship bracelets under a tree, swim, or even encounter a family of deer on the path to breakfast! Singers share cabins, compete for prizes for creative outfits during Spirit Days, and go on hikes to explore nature, watch sunsets, do arts and crafts, and share camp recitals and evening programs. By the time the last day of camp rolls around, the joy and memories are mixed with not wanting to leave. Join us this summer; we can’t wait to sing with you. Camp Dates Session 1: July 21 - July 26 Session 2: July 28 - August 2 Location: Since 2006, Choir Camp is located at Walker Creek Ranch in Marin County: The 1700-acre sleepaway camp site includes forest, chaparral, grassland, 20 miles of hiking trails, and a great 4-acre swimming hole! Cost: $1,775/week – Financial assistance is available. Save your spot now for Camp Joyful Voices: To find out more about Camp Joyful Voices and our other camp programs, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/camp or contact Camp Director Tate Bissinger at tbissinger@piedmontchoirs.org. Campers are excited for the Camp Concert where they show their parents what they learned. Reading the Piedmont Post is also an option at Choir Camp! Campers enjoy creating art and spending time with their new friends.

articles.text: Piedmont educator Chad Hamilton is bringing his beloved Play Ground Sports and Games Camp back for another exciting summer season. As a Havens School teacher and Piedmont native, Hamilton has been nurturing young athletes and fostering community connections through his summer programs for over a decade. “Through my time working A young athlete showcases her skills on the field during Play Ground Sports and Games Camp. The thrill of the chase! Campers dash across the field during an exciting game of Capture the Flag. with children in the competitive sports environment, I saw a need for sports to be inclusive and fun for all, not just the most gifted athletes,” explains Hamilton, who transitioned from teaching third grade to Physical Education at Havens School. “With this in mind, I created Play Ground Sports, where our philosophy is to ‘Build athletes from the (Play) ground up.’” Drawing from his own memories of summers spent in Piedmont’s parks and pools, Hamilton has crafted a program that emphasizes enjoyment over competition. The camp offers a dynamic mix of traditional sports like flag football, basketball, and soccer, alongside creative activities such as Star Wars-themed games, scavenger hunts, and building competitions. What sets this camp apart is its emphasis on unstructured play and personal growth. “It is on the playground that children are allowed to try new things and feel success and failure where there is nothing on the line. No awards, no pressure, and no parents watching,” Hamilton notes. “Play for the sake of play is something that is so often overlooked in youth sports today.” The program is staffed by an enthusiastic team of middle and high school athletes, many of whom are former campers themselves, creating a unique mentorship dynamic. Parents can expect their children to return home pleasantly tired, perhaps a bit dusty, and wearing big smiles – telltale signs of a day well spent in active, engaging play. Featured activities include crowd favorites like dodgeball and capture the flag, alongside innovative team-building exercises and creative games that keep children engaged while developing crucial social and athletic skills. Registration is offered through the Piedmont Recreation Department. For more information follow @play.ground.sports on Instagram or contact Hamilton directly at coachhamiltonofficial@gmail.com. Piedmont High’s No. 1 seeded boys’ soccer team is heading to the Division 4 North Coast Section semifinals. The pair of postseason wins sends the Highlanders to the NCS semifinals for the fifth consecutive year. “It should be six if we didn’t have that COVID year with no postseason,” Spencer said. “We were ranked ninth in the Bay Area. We haven’t had a fully healthy team in 3-4 weeks, which gave other guys more game experience,” he said. Saturday’s win over Bethel also marked a prestigious moment for senior Ravi Silverberg, who scored his 1,000th career point at the end of the second quarter. articles.text: Piedmont hosts 5th-place Final vs. No. 6 Salesian tonight The Highlanders’ No. 5 seeded girls’ basketball team lost in the first round of the North Coast Section Open Division playoffs. They were upended by No. 4 Cardinal Newman 51-45 in Santa Rosa on Thursday, February 20. “We just didn’t adjust well. That’s been one of our issues where we slow down and don’t adjust in games. Still, it’s great to be recognized as a top-six team in North Coast Section,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Playing in the NCS’ top echelon of teams gives them one more game as an automatic berth in the CIF State Tournament. They will host No. 6 Salesian tonight, February 26, for the 5th-place Final. Against the Cardinals, the Highlanders played a strong first half, and led 24-17 through a low-scoring first half. However, the wheels came off for PHS in the third quarter when they were outscored 20-7, including a 16-point run by Cardinal Newman to jump ahead 37-31 to start the fourth. At the time of the Cardinals’ scoring run, Piedmont held a 31-28 lead. One consolation after the loss was the announcement that freshman Jenelle Solis was named the Western Alameda Count Conference’s Co-Most Valuable Player. Piedmont looks ahead to tonight’s game with Salesian which will be played at home in Binks Rawlings Gym. It may be an advantageous matchup for the Highlanders to Jenelle Solis scored 12 points against Cardinal Newman. She was recently named the League Co-MVP. articles.text: Piedmont’s top-seeded girls’ soccer team saw its Division 4 North Coast Section postseason come to an end on Saturday, February 22 after falling 2-0 to No. 8 Pinole Valley at Witter Field. PHS couldn’t find the same offensive fluidity as in their 5-1 win over No. 16 College Prep on Wednesday, February 19. “We didn’t do enough to win it tonight. It sort of summarized our season. We’ve had some close games. We didn’t really have any clear chances tonight,” added coach Dan Chubbock. The Highlanders struggled to create dangerous chances against the Spartans, but many passes went too long or were swept up by defenders. “It probably could’ve been a nil-nil type of game,” Chubbock noted. ”We’re just disappointed, especially being the No. 1 seed, but it wasn’t to be. Their center mid was good and their forward was causing us some problems. Their goalie had a good game too,” Both teams remained deadlocked through most of the first half, but Pinole Valley scored the first goal right before halftime at 40+2 minutes. It came when the Spartans sent in a long free kick, allowing the ball to bounce before an attacker pushed it into net. Pinole’s final goal came with about 10 minutes left in the game in the 70th minute on a similar play, where a long free kick was allowed to bounce and fall to an open attacker. Piedmont finished its season with a 7-2-10 (W-T-L) record as it dealt with several key injuries to key players Elsa Wallway, Darcy McKee, Louisa Symkowick, Juliana Thornborrow, Ryo Woltag, and Eliza Hammond. Standout junior Miranda Liu, who was the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year, returned to play against Pinole Valley. “Obviously, the injuries this year held us back. But still, we can’t use it as an excuse. We were the No. 1 seed in Div. 4 and we were fairly ranked. I think we all felt like we could have made a really good run, but we didn’t execute the things we do well,” Chubbock said. Looking ahead, the team will lose 10 seniors to graduation. It could potentially bring back players who earned key minutes, like freshmen Kyla Williams, Teah Suhr and Ayla Blanford, sophomores Wallway and Chloe Toyama, and juniors Elia Kwong, Stephanie Lee, and McKee. No.1 PHS loses 2-0 to No. 8 Pinole Valley In the first half, Kwong had a shot on target in the second minute. Hannah Sullivan then nearly found Woltag from a corner in the 11th minute, but her shot went wide. From there, both teams traded possession without any clear chances until PVHS scored from its long free kick right before halftime. In the second half, Kwong had a shot from atop the penalty area go narrowly wide of the left post in the 45th. Liu had a shot also go wide four minutes later. After several trades of possession, Pinole Valley drew its long free kick that led to their goal. From about 45 yards, they sent in a long pass that was mishandled, falling straight to an attacker for the finishing goal. 5-1 over No. 16 College Prep Williams scored Piedmont’s first goal in the 25th minute when College Prep’s keeper sent a slopped pass to her fullback. Williams pounced on possession, sending in a shot from the left side. College Prep tied the match in the 30th minute, but the Highlanders scored just two minutes later when Thornborrow recovered a ball in the box, launching a shot over the keeper to the far post. pages.text: Wednesday, February 26, 2025 13 Girls Basketball falls to No. 4 Cardinal Newman Piedmont hosts 5th-place Final vs. No. 6 Salesian tonight By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlanders’ No. 5 seeded girls’ basketball team lost in the first round of the North Coast Section Open Division playoffs. They were upended by No. 4 Cardinal Newman 51-45 in Santa Rosa on Thursday, February 20. “We just didn’t adjust well. That’s been one of our issues where we slow down and don’t adjust in games. Still, it’s great to be recognized as a top-six team in North Coast Section,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Playing in the NCS’ top echelon of teams gives them one more game as an automatic berth in the CIF State Tournament. They will host No. 6 Salesian tonight, February 26, for the 5th-place Final. Against the Cardinals, the Highlanders played a strong first half, and led 24-17 through a low-scoring first half. However, the wheels came off for PHS in the third quarter when they were outscored 20-7, including a 16-point run by Cardinal Newman to jump ahead 37-31 to start the fourth. At the time of the Cardinals’ scoring run, Piedmont held a 31-28 lead. One consolation after the loss was the announcement that freshman Jenelle Solis was named the Western Alameda Count Conference’s Co-Most Valuable Player. Piedmont looks ahead to tonight’s game with Salesian which will be played at home in Binks Rawlings Gym. It may be an advantageous matchup for the Highlanders to Jenelle Solis scored 12 points against Cardinal Newman. She was recently named the League Co-MVP. Staff Photos Piedmont fell 51-45 to No. 4 Cardinal Newman. They host No. 6 Salesian for the NCS Open Division 5th-place Final tonight, February 26. solidify its seeding going into the state tournament. The two sides have had two common opponents this year, Clayton Valley and Bishop O’Dowd. Salesian lost to Clayton Valley 61-40 on January 4, while the Highlanders beat them 61-52 in overtime on January 3. Salesian also lost to O’Dowd 67-47 on January 25, while Piedmont recently defeated the Dragons 50-47 on February 5. Game Recap Piedmont held a close 8-6 lead through a low-scoring first quarter and extended their advantage to 24-17 by halftime. However, Cardinal Newman outscore Piedmont 20-7 in the third with a 16-point run that stretched into the fourth quarter, up 37-31. Both teams traded 14 points in the final going, 51-45 Cardinal Newman. Piedmont didn’t do themselves any favors at the free throw line, missing 15 total shots from the stripe. The Highlanders’ 16-point second quarter had points by five different players. Andrea Martin had four points in the quarter, while Jenelle Solis had five points with a 3-pointer. Piedmont only converted four 3-pointers on the night. Final stats: Martin had a double-double with 10 points, 10 rebounds, two assists, and two blocks. Savannah Dennig had two rebounds and a steal. Solis had 12 points, three rebounds, and five assists. Shakila Zuberi had five points and four rebounds. Taylor White had five points, seven rebounds, an assist, and three steals Briana Webb had nine points, four rebounds, and two assists. Cleo Afsar had four points and a rebound. PHS couldn’t find the same offensive fluidity as in their 5-1 win over No. 16 College Prep on Wednesday, February 19. “We didn’t do enough to win it tonight. It sort of summarized our season. We’ve had some close games. We didn’t really have any clear chances tonight,” added coach Dan Chubbock. The Highlanders struggled to create dangerous chances against the Spartans, but many passes went too long or were swept up by defenders. “It probably could’ve been a nil-nil type of game,” Chubbock noted. ”We’re just disappointed, especially being the No. 1 seed, but it wasn’t to be. Their center mid was good and their forward was causing us some problems. Their goalie had a good game too,” Both teams remained deadlocked through most of the first half, but Pinole Valley scored the first goal right before halftime at 40+2 minutes. It came when the Spartans sent in a long free kick, allowing the ball to bounce before an attacker pushed it into net. Pinole’s final goal came with about 10 minutes left in the game in the 70th minute on a similar play, where a long free kick was allowed to bounce and fall to an open attacker. Piedmont finished its season with a 7-2-10 (W-T-L) record as it dealt with several key injuries to key players Elsa Wallway, Darcy McKee, Louisa Symkowick, Juliana Thornborrow, Ryo Woltag, and Eliza Hammond. Standout junior Miranda Liu, who was the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year, returned to play against Pinole Valley. “Obviously, the injuries this year held us back. But still, we can’t use it as an excuse. We were the No. 1 seed in Div. 4 and we were fairly ranked. I think we all felt like we could have made a really good run, but we didn’t execute the things we do well,” Chubbock said. Looking ahead, the team will lose 10 seniors to graduation. It could potentially bring back players who earned key minutes, like freshmen Kyla Williams, Teah Suhr and Ayla Blanford, sophomores Wallway and Chloe Toyama, and juniors Elia Kwong, Stephanie Lee, and McKee. No.1 PHS loses 2-0 to No. 8 Pinole Valley In the first half, Kwong had a shot on target in the second minute. Hannah Sullivan then nearly found Woltag from a corner in the 11th minute, but her shot went wide. From there, both teams traded possession without any clear chances until PVHS scored from its long free kick right before halftime. In the second half, Kwong had a shot from atop the penalty area go narrowly wide of the left post in the 45th. Liu had a shot also go wide four minutes later. After several trades of possession, Pinole Valley drew its long free kick that led to their goal. From about 45 yards, they sent in a long pass that was mishandled, falling straight to an attacker for the finishing goal. 5-1 over No. 16 College Prep Williams scored Piedmont’s first goal in the 25th minute when College Prep’s keeper sent a slopped pass to her fullback. Williams pounced on possession, sending in a shot from the left side. College Prep tied the match in the 30th minute, but the Highlanders scored just two minutes later when Thornborrow recovered a ball in the box, launching a shot over the keeper to the far post. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team returned to toe the line on Saturday, February 22 at the Skyline Invitational, hosted by Skyline HS in Oakland. The Highlanders will have some key athletes missing, like distance runner Xander Schulte-Sasse and girls’ sprinter Breah Bell, but they return a good bulk of talent. “We’re returning 27 of our top 30-point scorers on the boys’ side.” coach Pouyan Assadi said. “Our depth is there and our experience is there. The quantity of rising stars on the boys’ side is fascinating and I’m eager to see who steps up to take the lead. On the girls’ side, the heartbeat of the team is in the 800 and 1600 races,” he added. The 2025 season also marks a return to Witter Field for the track and field team after missing the majority of offseason training last year as Witter Field’s renovation was delayed for nearly one year. Assadi pointed out how the return of their home track has already shown improvement in training and also to limiting injuries. “We are on our own home turf, walking to and from the field from our houses. Our injuries have plummeted and we have access to our weight room. It is so nice to be home,” Assadi said. Skyline results At Saturday’s meet, Piedmont’s boys’ 4x100 relay team won with a time of 44.41 in a close finish with Berkeley and George Washington. Piedmont runners were sophomore Eric Venner, senior Sam Shelby, sophomore Rehan Mumtaz, and junior Maddox Ma. Shelby enters an important season after missing most of 2024 with an injury. Ella Yasar qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions in three events last year and is a key returner on the track and field team. Sam Shelby looks ahead to his senior year in track. He helped Piedmont’s 4x100 relay team win at the Skyline Invitational on February 22. “Sam has a chance to rewrite the entire sprinting record book. He’s keen on making an impact this year. He has a lot of opportunities at the collegiate level in football and track. He understands if he puts a nice season together, those opportunities will continue to grow,” Assadi said. Venner and Ma were members of last year’s 4x400 relay team that qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions. Mumtaz is another runner making an impact. With their talent available, Assadi expects Piedmont’s sprinting teams to be among their strong points. “Eric is one of my favorite people to coach because he fully understands what we’re trying to do and he takes it all in. Rehan is also rising with him and Maddox Ma had a substantial PR on the boys’ side on Saturday. That crew is going to do some damage,” Assadi said with a smile. Senior Miguel Long is another key returner. He typically competes in Piedmont’s jumping events and was last year’s leading point scorer for the team. On Saturday, Long competed in three events. He was third in the long jump with a distance of 21 feet, 11 inches; second in the triple jump in 42 feet, 7 inches; and second in the 110-meter hurdles in 16.25 seconds. “Miguel led the team in scoring the previous two years,” Assadi said. Distance runner Sebastien Swain will also make an impact. He’s coming off a strong fall season on the cross-country team, where he qualified for the State Championship in Fresno. At Saturday’s event in Skyline, Swain was second of 57 runners in the 800 meters with a time of 1:59.15. Miguel Long typically competes in the jumping events. He’s another senior on this year’s team. “We all know what Sebastien did as a freshman. Last week, he opened up with a sub two-minute half-mile already,” Assadi said. The girls’ team has some talented distance runners. Sophomores Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray also made headlines last fall for qualifying for the State Championship. “This group of girls’ work ethic is admirable, It’s not a surprise to me that someone like Leighton had a big cross- country season. She’s a heck of a competitor,” Assadi said. Yasar will be a senior leader on the team. She reached last year’s Meet of Champions in three events, the 300-meter hurdles, the 4x100, and 4x400 relay teams. “Ella qualified for the Meet of Champions in three separate events, which is pretty rare to do. With her experience, knowledge, and understanding of my coaching style and the combination of her health, we’re expecting big things from her this year,” Assadi said. Another returner to the field events is thrower Alina Shahid, a senior. At Saturday’s event she was second in the discus with a distance of 85 feet, 7 inches. She also was eighth of 21 in the shot put with 22 feet, 6 inches. With the return of Witter Field, Piedmont will host the first two Western Alameda County Conference Center Meets of the season on March 12 and March 27. articles.text: Staff Photos Girls Lacrosse and coach Carlton Chan are back for the 2025 season. Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse returns for the 2025 season as defending Western Alameda County Conference champions. They finished last season with a 14-5 record and reached the second round of the North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seed before losing 9-7 to No. 4 Acalanes. They bring back several key players from last year’s team but will need to fill a void created by the graduation of attacker Ruby Guzdar and middie Hailey Marshburn. “We had really fun players last year and losing them is huge. But the biggest thing for this year is rebuilding out defense. Although it’s a rebuilding year, every year is that way,” said veteran coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont will have experience on its side. Fourteen of its 19 players are seniors. Chan will have senior leaders including Friedie Schickedanz, Chloe Graham, and Luisa Cole, while junior Peyton Watson is another multiyear varsity player. All four players are co-captains this season. “They are outstanding players, so we’re going to be pretty good. This group of girls has played in our system for a while, so they are very familiar with it, but they will have to step up without a Ruby or Hailey to really move the ball,” Chan said. Chan compared this year’s group to the 2019 team that won the D2 NCS title That team relied on their athletic ability to keep teams off balance. “This year, we’re going to go back in time to our 2019 year where there was a lot of cutting and fundamentals. The girls are really good at pick-and-rolls, so we can get a lot of assists. Chloe and Payton also cut really well,” Chan said. Comparing to the 2019 squad, Schickedanz will mirror the school’s All-Time assist leader, Sadie Tschider, who was known for flicking accurate passes to cutters. “We’re looking to get a lot of assists from Friedie. We’re teaching her to be a lot like Sadie, and she’s doing a great job,” Chan said. In goal, senior Sophie Santander steps in as the starter. It allows former goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter to play as a defender on the field. “Sophie Santander is playing tremendous. She was on JV last year and we brought her up,” said Chan. “On the field, Annika is a tremendous player as well. It’s really fun to see her worked into the starting lineup, she earned that spot. She’s transformed into a defender really well.” The Highlanders are looking to compete with Berkeley and Bishop O’Dowd for the league title. Berkeley went 8-10 last year and Piedmont defeated O’Dowd 8-7 in last year’s WACC championship. The Dragons bring back Cornell-commit Lucy Yu, the daughter of former Piedmont High boys’ coach Al Yu. “Not to jinx myself, but we have a lot more returners and better balance than some of the teams. I think Berkeley will be tough and O’Dowd still has Lucy, but they aren’t quite as balanced. I think for our team, everyone can make an impact,” Chan said. Piedmont played its first game of the season on Tuesday, February 25 at Washington in Fremont. They play again at Moreau Catholic in Hayward on February 27 before playing its first home game against Amador Valley the following day, February 28. Friedie Schickedanz is a key player in Piedmont’s attack. Luisa Cole is among this year’s captains.

articles.text: After years of success, Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team has been undergoing a lot of change since 2023. After going 8-6 in 2024 and suffering its first ever season without a Western Alameda County Conference, the Highlanders are looking to recapture their mojo. Entering the fold as new head coach is Paul Pappas, a Piedmont High graduate from the Class of 2020 and a member of the school’s last NCS title in 2019. “We want to bring Piedmont lacrosse back to what it was when I was here,” said Pappas. That starts with the culture and getting the community behind the team again. Honestly, winning is a big part of it too and we need to start winning again,” Pappas said. Pappas will fill an essential void. The coaching position became available after the school’s initial choice at head coach backed out of the job. “One of the beautiful things about Piedmont lacrosse is most of the athletes have been playing together since they were eight years old. I just feel lucky to be in an opportunity where the timing all worked out, where I get to give back to a program that gave me so much,” Pappas said. Joining Pappas’ coaching staff will be 2020 classmate Georgie Brayer as defensive coordinator, and Rex Peters, also a 2020 classmate as offensive coordinator “I have two former teammates from the NCS team on our coaching staff. Georgie is one of my ride-or-die best friends since high school. He’s running our defense. Rex Peters is spearheading the offense,” Pappas said. It all makes for a “Made in Piedmont” type of team to return to its winning-culture. “It’s all about making these players want to be there and have fun.,” Pappas said. Pappas was the Highlanders’ goalie when he played for the school before attending the University of Arizona. When I went to school in Arizona, I helped out in a lot of youth lacrosse programs. I worked for Goalie Smith for about a year and helped out in their camps developing goalies. But the big thing we are trying to implement is just culture. The Xs and Os will come, but off the bat, our big thing is guiding these young boys into proper young men,” Pappas said. This year’s team will have sophomore Connor Fredericks leading the attack. He also doubles as their faceoff specialist. articles.text: Landmark exhibition of China’s Picasso The Asian Art Museum of San Francisco’s is now showing Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink, a landmark exhibition of the renowned Chinese ink painter Qi Baishi (1864–1957), now through April 7. This exhibition marks the 160th anniversary of the artist’s birth and features 42 works on paper lent by the Beijing Fine Art Academy, where Qi served as its first honorary director. This is the first time these works have been presented in the United States. Born during the late Qing Dynasty, Qi was positioned at a unique place in history, living through some of the most transformative shifts in China’s political and cultural history. Despite this changing landscape, the artist’s accessible subject matter and virtuosic style earned him immense respect and popularity, both at home and abroad. In 1960, Qi became the first Chinese artist ever to receive a solo exhibition at the de Young Museum in San Francisco. Sometimes referred to as China’s Picasso, his pieces have achieved record-breaking prices at auctions worldwide — as high as $141 million in 2017 for Twelve Landscape Screens (1925) – underscoring his profound impact on the art market and his status as an international cultural icon. Qi’s legendary career saw the artist rise from humble origins as a peasant carpenter to become one of China’s most revered and best-selling painters. Celebrated for its whimsical approach and technical virtuosity, his works bring to life subjects drawn from the natural world and everyday life. Iconic images of shrimp and crab, among other motifs, reflect his ability to find hidden visual joys and transform the mundane into the magical, resonating with viewers across generations. “Qi Baishi’s technical abilities and expressionistic approach imbue his art with a spiritual quality, inviting viewers to contemplate the deeper significance of everyday motifs,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Barbara and Gerson Bakar Curator of Chinese Art. “His work resonates so widely with audiences because he not only captures his subjects but Flower and Pug Moths, Album of Elaborate Works of Fine Brushwork Insects, No. 1, 1949, Qi Baishi. See the Asian Art Museum’s landmark exhibition of Qi, “China’s Picasso,” the renowned ink painter Qi Baishi, now through April 7. also seeks to express their spirit through calligraphic, spontaneous strokes, something that requires master brushwork.” Considered the most popular painter of 20th-century China, Qi’s semi-abstract, minimalist approach to ink painting not only bridged traditional Chinese ink art with modernist tendencies, but also left a lasting impact on global art movements. He was publicly admired by Picasso and served as an ink art teacher to celebrated Japanese American artist and architect Isamu Noguchi. Today, scholars credit Qi’s combination of mundane subject matter and innovative, multifaceted techniques as having revitalized traditional Chinese ink painting for the modern era. “Qi Baishi’s quotidian subject matter and whimsical, playful style made his art incredibly accessible to audiences at the time, making him the first Chinese painter to capture the attention of American audiences,” said Rob Mintz, Chief Curator at the Asian Art Museum. “His ability to capture the beauty in the ordinary contributed to his growing popularity inside and outside of China, a legacy that continues to thrive today.” In conjunction with the exhibition, visitors will have the opportunity to engage with Qi’s legacy through digital and tactile experiences. Guests can digitally “paint” at a desk at the exhibition that renders their own virtual “brushstrokes” in the style of Qi. Visitors can also take a small piece of the exhibition home with a Letters from the Artist wall, on which guests can find replicas of letters that Qi wrote to his patrons and friends one century ago. articles.text: De Young opens rare 1963-64 Paul McCartney photo exhibition Paul McCartney. Self-portrait. London, 1963. Paul McCartney Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm presents over 250 personal photos by McCartney, alongside video clips and archival materials, at San Francisco’s de Young Museum this Saturday through July 6. Nearly 60 years after The Beatles performed their final concert at San Francisco’s Candlestick Park, Beatlemania is back in the Bay in a photo exhibit this Saturday, March 31 through July 6. Organized by the National Portrait Gallery of London, and presented exclusively in California at the de Young Museum, Paul McCartney Photographs 1963– 64: Eyes of the Storm will present more than 250 personal photos by Paul McCartney, alongside video clips and archival materials that offer a behind-the-scenes look into the meteoric rise of the world’s most celebrated band. Eyes of the Storm captures a period from December 1963 through February 1964 when The Beatles performed in concert halls across England and in the United States. McCartney’s images reveal the intensity of life on tour as The Beatles were whisked from concerts to hotels, trailed by enthusiastic fans from New York to Miami. Photographs of screaming crowds and paparazzi illustrate the sheer magnitude of the group’s superstardom. In stark contrast, behind-closed-doors images captured by McCartney highlight the humor and individuality of the band members on their days off. Eyes of the Storm invites visitors to witness The Beatles’ journey to stardom, from local venues in Liverpool to the Ed Sullivan Show and worldwide acclaim. McCartney’s photographs of the four band members existed as unprinted negatives and contact sheets for 60 years. Rediscovered in the artist’s personal archive in 2020, these images offer new insight into the band, their fans and the early 1960s, as seen through his eyes. “In this exhibition, we glimpse McCartney both behind and in front of the lens, as he bears witness to a pivotal cultural moment through the camera with a keen artistic eye,” said organizing curator Sally Martin Katz. “From portraiture to landscapes and documentary shots, McCartney demonstrates a deep understanding of the formal styles prevalent in early 1960s photography. Throughout the exhibition, nods to New Wave, documentary filmmaking, and photojournalism underscore McCartney’s multifaceted approach to capturing the spirit of the time,” she added. “In Eyes of the Storm, recently unearthed photographs by McCartney provide a rare time capsule of The Beatles’ world at the moment of their extraordinary rise to fame,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “It is a revelation to discover McCartney’s proficiency as a photographer, documenting everything from the band’s quieter moments and friendships to the ‘Beatlemania’ of the time.” The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive) is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. Tickets ($20 general, $17 seniors, $11 students, youth free) are available at famsf.org or at 888-901-6645.

articles.text: The San José Museum of Art announces the opening of the Museum’s first exhibit dedicated to displaying works from its own collection, starting Friday, March 7. Drawing on the Museum’s holdings of over 2,700 works, the inaugural installation Tending and Dreaming: Stories from the Collection will be on view for one year and will include veteran artworks from the collection such as Louise Nevelson’s Sky Cathedral (1957) and Hung Liu’s Resident Alien (1988), as well as recent acquisitions of major artworks by Tishan Hsu, Yolanda López and Sarah Sze, among other artists. Tending and Dreaming will feature paintings, sculptures, photographs, videos, and installations by nearly fifty artists from the Bay Area and beyond. “Since SJMA began collecting art in the 1990s, what began with a regional focus has evolved into a collection that transcends geographic boundaries, tracking the ruptures of the digital age and the complexities of our collective cultural, political, and social struggles and triumphs,” said S. Sayre Batton, Oshman Executive Director at SJMA. “We are thrilled to take the next step in this journey by dedicating permanent gallery space to the stories within our collection,” she added. “By highlighting artists as storytellers, this installation invites visitors to see the Museum not just as a repository of art, but as a dynamic, living space where culture is continually created, interpreted and reimagined.” This marks the first time since the Museum’s collecting program began in 1973 under the guidance of local artists, that dedicated and permanent galleries will showcase the breadth and depth of its holdings. Organized into six thematic groupings, Tending and Dreaming offers visitors a new framework for engaging with the powerful narratives woven through the artworks. The first section considers what it means to be of a place, bringing together artworks that engage local materials such as adobe in the case of performance artist Rafa Esparza and recorded local histories as with interdisciplinary artist Christine Howard Sandoval. The second grouping features artworks that grapple with the stakes of self-making, such as when one migrates to another country as explored by Shilpa Gupta, or by attending to ancestral histories as with the work of Binh Danh. Featuring artists such as Chitra Ganesh, Robert Arneson and Guadalupe Rosales, the third grouping includes artworks that reclaim or disregard dominant perspectives in American culture. The next section explores the connectivity facilitated by technology, such as in Christine Sun Kim’s sound sculpture with recorded lullabies composed in collaboration with an extended network of parent friends, and Martha Atienza’s poetic address to globally rising sea levels. The fifth grouping features a broad range of approaches to engaging the more-than-human world — such as by exploring the cultural continuities of human bodies and land in the case of Laura Aguilar’s photographs, or by attending to the lifespans and intelligences of other organisms as in Gail Wight’s time-lapse video of slime mold. Featuring artworks by Candida Alvarez, Lee Mullican and Harry Powers among others, the final section explores how artists evoke and give form to experiences that are otherwise often unnoticed. The San José Museum of Art (110 South Market Street, San Jose) is open 4 p.m. to 9p.m. Thursdays, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Fridays and 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturdays and Sundays. Tickets ($20 general, $15 senior, free for youth 17 and under, free for college students and teachers with ID) are available at sjmusart.org. See The Only Door I Can Open: Women Exposing Prison through Art, an immersive multimedia exhibition co-curated from within prison, at San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts now through June 22. San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts presents a multimedia exhibition exploring the experience of incarcerated women, now through June 22. The exhibition is inspired by a poem by co-curator Tomiekia Johnson, in which she describes her prison bed as “the only door I can open,” while she reflects on her experience of being incarcerated. The Only Door I Can Open: Women Exposing Prison through Art is an immersive multimedia exhibition co-curated from within prison by Johnson and Chantell-Jeannette Black. For the exhibition, Johnson and Black asked eight currently and formerly incarcerated artists to create an artwork that reflects on their relationship to their bed. Within the prison system, a person’s bed is one of the only spaces where they can be alone. For some, the bed is a place of safety and privacy, while for others it is a space of isolation and angst. The exhibition features an array of artworks in diverse media — including murals, paintings and audio narratives — as well as an immersive installation which mirrors a prison cell at Central California Women’s Facility at Chowchilla, where the curators reside. For both Johnson and Black, the exhibition offers a powerful opportunity to encourage visitors to think more deeply about the problematic nature of the prison system itself and take action to enact change. “Prison may be a sentence because of crimes committed, but for those in it, prison is also a state of being,” said Chantell-Jeannette Black. “Art is our platform for human rights, and the outlet through which our voices may be heard. We want viewers to feel inspired to change and grow, to become more than what they were before viewing this artwork.” “I hope that this exhibition allows visitors to picture themselves in my shoes, my bed, on my bunk, feeling the feelings I feel,” said Johnson. “I would like the solution side of people to awaken. I want people to walk away from the exhibit feeling flooded with differing emotions.” “It is important for us to bring our work to where people live, to the neighborhoods and communities that are impacted by the topics we are addressing, and to center the voices of those who are living this experience,” said Jo Kreiter, founder of curation partner company Flyaway Prosponsored by the PEF COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT COMMITTEE Tuesday, March 11 Welcome Reception 5:00 - 6:30 PM $50 per person Piedmont Community Hall Parent Ed Talk 7:30 - 8:30 PM $25 per person Alan Harvey Theater Best Selling Author & PBS Host Wednesday, April 16 7:30 - 9:00 PM Early Bird Tickets: $50 per person Private Piedmont Home

By Selen Ozturk San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts presents a multimedia exhibition exploring the experience of incarcerated women, now through June 22. The exhibition is inspired by a poem by co-curator Tomiekia Johnson, in which she describes her prison bed as “the only door I can open,” while she reflects on her experience of being incarcerated. For the exhibition, Johnson and Black asked eight currently and formerly incarcerated artists to create an artwork that reflects on their relationship to their bed. articles.text: Singer-songwriter Martha Redbone leads This Land Is Our Land, a roots music collaboration with the American Patchwork Quartet at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall this Friday, February 28. Roots music singer and songwriter Martha Redbone will lead This Land Is Our Land, a new collaboration between her Martha Redbone Roots Project and the genre-defying American Patchwork Quartet this Friday, February 28 at 8 p.m. at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall. Redbone draws on her heritage as a southeastern Cherokee/ Choctaw and Black American woman to craft songs that celebrate the human spirit, infused with the folk and blues sounds of her childhood in the Appalachian Mountains of Kentucky. Led by Grammy-winning guitarist and vocalist Clay Ross, American Patchwork Quartet is on a self- professed “mission to reclaim the immigrant soul of American roots music.” The ensemble’s repertoire merges folk songs with jazz, country music and sounds from West Africa and Asia, featuring members Falguni Shah (Falu), vocalist; Yasushi Nakamura, bassist; and Clarence Penn, drummer. The Martha Redbone Roots Project consists of Redbone, vocalist and percussionist; Aaron Whitby, pianist and vocalist; Charlie Burnham, violinist and vocalistt; and Fred Cash, bassist and vocalist. The performance continues this season’s Illuminations programming, which explores the idea of “fractured history” through eight performances. Through this series, producer Cal Performances investigates collective memory and the complex evolution of historical narratives to consider what role the performing arts might play in restoring nuance to our understanding of the past, and how that understanding shapes our present and future. For more details for this and other performances in the series, visit calperformances.org/illuminations-2024-25. The group remains ensemble-in-residence at the UW-Madison School of Music and resident quartet of the on-campus Chazen Museum of Art, performing regularly on the concert series of both institutions. articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company has announced the program for its fourth Dancing Moons Festival on May 4, an annual celebration of Asian American and Pacific Islander artists. This year the company premieres a major new work inspired by the lives of detainees at Angel Island, the United States’ main immigration facility on the West Coast from 1910 to 1940. In collaboration with the Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation and Angel Island Parks and Recreation, the Angel Island Project features the work of seven choreographers, including Natasha Adorlee, Phil Chan, Lawrence Chen, Feng Ye, Elaine Kudo, Ashley Thopiah, and Wei Wang. In advance of the premiere at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland, on Sunday, May 4, Oakland Ballet Company will present an introduction to the Angel Island Project at the Angel Island Immigration Station. This hour-long event will include a short lecture by Ed Tepporn, executive director of the Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation, on the history of the station, followed by a preview performance of the Angel Island Project and a brief Q&A session with the artists. This preview event will take place on the final two Saturdays in March: March 22 and 29 at 12:45 p.m. Due to the constraints of the site, audiences are limited to 70 people. Tickets ($67- $75) are now on sale at oaklandballet. org/performances-events/angel_ island_project. Ferry passage to Angel Island must be purchased separately. At the premiere on May 4, Oakland Ballet Company will be accompanied by the Del Sol Quartet, under the direction of Charlton Lee, and members of Volti, a choral ensemble, under the direction of Robert Geary. Dr. Wei Cheng will conduct. Tickets, $43 – $86, are now on sale. Featuring an 80-minute oratorio scored for string quartet, 16 singers and a narrator, the music, commissioned by Del Sol in 2020, was composed by Huang Ruo, one of the world’s leading young composers. Born and raised in China, Ruo currently Photo by John Hefti AL Abraham (left), Jazmine Quezada, Lawrence Chen (floor), Florrie Geller (standing) and Ashley Thopiah in Oakland Ballet’s performance of The Seascape by Feng Ye. Photo by John Hefti Jazmine Quezada in Natasha Adorlee’s Last Chinaman from the Titanic, one of seven sections of the Angel Island Project. resides in New York City where he teaches at the Mannes School of Music. This fall, the San Francisco Opera will premiere Ruo’s newest opera, The Monkey King. “With captured imaginations, we take flight on a journey of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved into the walls by detainees at the Angel Island Immigration Station,” said Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig. “The Angel Island Project helps trace who we all are today by remembering our origins and the many perilous journeys made by our ancestors.”

It is interesting to note that the United States was the first country to offer concerts in churches. In Europe, this never happened. The gigantic cathedral of Saint Mary’s in San Francisco is one of those unique concert spaces. A concert on Sunday afternoon offered interesting performers, as well as a very interesting program. My wife and I enjoyed the music but were disappointed by the dearth of people in the audience. The featured group was the Quantum Trio which included Wendy Loder (soprano and violinist), Joel Cohen (cello), and Jeanette Wilkin Tietze (piano). All of these musicians s have exemplary credentials. I often wonder what it takes to get a full audience. It is sad that huge audiences are often drawn by over-publicized performers, who fail to deliver high level musicianship. Throughout the concert the performances were very sensitive. articles.text: Kids will love How to Train Your Dragon. It’s one nifty movie. Let’s start not at the beginning but with an inspired and breathtaking scene: a young Viking named Hiccup, seated securely on the back of Toothless, an ebony dragon, soars through the clouds in a prolonged flight that is breathtaking. The colors are lush and gorgeous, the sky a startlingly blue in contrast to the enormous cumulus clouds. Hiccup, eyes wide, is exhilarated and terrified. This scene, like so many in this film, is testimony to the depth and breadth of the imagination of the filmmakers, and graphically illustrates how stateof-the-art animation, combined with the technology of 3-D, has made quantum strides in the last several years. Of course, neither technology nor 3-D can save a film if the story lacks serious mojo. How to Train Your Dragon has all the right stuff: a sweet if recognizable story that will resonate with youngsters, tweens and likely early teens. And the characters are, to a person, perfect. Briefly, there’s young Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), the son of Stoick the Vast (Gerard Butler), who lives on the small island of Berk, off the coast of Scotland. For 300 years dragons have been attacking their village, making off with their livestock. The Vikings have fought back and along the way developed an abiding hatred for and fear of dragons. Hiccup, a newbie adolescent, rebelling against his chieftain father and his community, resists learning to fight dragons. Stoic is both frustrated and angry with his son. Clearly Hiccup, lean in stature (the Vikings are all more than hefty), and not inclined to fight back when the dragons attack, is not cut out to be a dragon slayer. articles.text: Troop 4 Open House on March 3 As proud members of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 4, we’d like to share what makes the troop so special. Being part of Troop 4 has been one of the most rewarding experiences of our lives. Every meeting, every camping trip, and every community service project has taught us something new about nature, teamwork, and ourselves. “Troop 4 is amazing, filled with various activities and adventures to go on. Personally, I enjoy Troop 4 because of the many opportunities to go out and explore, talk to people, and work on requirements. It provides an overall friendly and welcoming atmosphere, and the outings we go on are a joy to be in. People here are all very kind, supportive, and constructive, and it is an amazing Troop through and through, for anyone interested in joining,” said Patrol Leader, Francis Guo From our very first day, we were captivated by the sense of adventure that filled our meetings and outings. we’ve hiked rugged trails, set up camp under endless starry skies, and learned invaluable outdoor skills like map reading and knot tying. Each adventure challenges us in different ways and deepens our love for the great outdoors. Whether it’s navigating a tricky path or mastering a new survival skill, every experience pushes us to grow and become more confident. “Troop 4 is a small troop which gives a lot of personal attention to the Scouts,” said Scoutmaster Eric Mellers. “We’re scout-led, which gives scouts a lot of opportunities. Scouts get to decide what we do, and it really allows us to do things that would be difficult as a larger troop. But we still offer a full program, we still have regular trips, and we’re trying to have a lot of fun”. One of the best parts of being a member of Troop 4 is the hands-on learning. We’ve had the opportunity to learn essential skills, from first aid and wilderness cooking to leadership and problem-solving. These skills aren’t just for the outdoors; they’re lessons that apply to everyday life, teaching us to face challenges head-on and trust our abilities. “My daughter visited all troop open houses. She knew right away that Troop 4 was the right one for her,” noted parent organizer Stacy Lau. “She was drawn to how fun and casual everything was. She could just come in and let out some steam. Some of her den mates joined another troop, but Troop 4 feels more laid back. The activities were a lot of fun, I really enjoyed getting to know the parents. It felt much more welcoming to her and had much more of a laid-back atmosphere”. What truly sets our troop apart is the sense of family and camaraderie among us. We’ve made friends here who share our love for adventure and who always have our back, both in the wild and out in everyday life. Our weekly meetings, group projects, and campfire evenings are more than just activities – they’re moments where we support each other, celebrate our victories, and learn from our mistakes together. “I think it’s been great. The size of the troop means that everything is very intimate and that everyone has a chance to talk to everyone. The parents are all very involved, and the scouts guide themselves, which offers opportunities to the scouts to do more things,” said parent organizer Tarun Nagpal. Being in Boy Scout Troop 4 has taught us so much about leadership. Every expedition and every group challenge gives us a chance to step up and help guide our fellow scouts. We’ve learned that leadership isn’t about being the loudest voice; it’s about listening, making thoughtful decisions, Photo from an overnight kayaking trip to Tomales Bay, 2024 White Water Rafting on the American River,Septemeber 2024 and inspiring others through your actions. These experiences have prepared us for future challenges, both in scouting and in life. “It’s fun, and everybody is very nice, and there’s fun to camp out, as a girl in the Boy Scout, I don’t feel any different, and I don’t feel the outdoor activities are too challenging, except when it rains! I can also learn a lot from the older scouts”. – Violet Shapp “As a young scout, troop 4 was very welcoming to me, and a lot of fun doing all the activities there were a lot of older scouts to support me, now, as a troop leader, I feel like taking a turn to support these young scouts. Now it’s their journey, and they get to experience the same fun I had as a younger scout. As a smaller troop, we get to focus more on individual scouts and their experiences,” said Troop 4 leader Jerry Yu. If you’re looking for an opportunity to explore the outdoors, learn valuable life skills, and build friendships that last a lifetime, we can’t recommend Troop 4 enough. Joining our troop opened up a world of adventure for us, and we know it can do the same for you. Whether you’re a seasoned adventurer or just curious about the Boy Scouts, there’s a place for you here. We invite you to experience the excitement, learning, and sense of belonging that we’ve found in Troop 4. Your journey to discovery, leadership, and lifelong friendships begins here, and we can’t wait to see you at the Troop 4 Open House, which is happening on March 3 at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, Havens School, 325 Highland Ave., Piedmont, from 7:30-8:30 p.m. Piedmont Scout Camporee 2024 Regular meeting at the PHS Student Center for Game Night in March 2024 Scouting for Food drive, November 2024

A drizzle turned into a light rain for the Walking on Wednesdays group, but it was not enough to stop 41 walkers and four K-9 best friends from being at the Exedra and enjoying their weekly walk. In the 1990s the house was raised to add a second floor. Today, there is a white picket fence and two inviting chairs in the front yard. The group could have gone straight up Howard to Lake Avenue and Beach School, but despite the light rain, they wanted to see and learn about the homes on Nace. In 1906, Laura Fenton, the granddaughter of the founder of Fenton’s Creamery, married Maxwell Franck, a young civil engineer, and they moved into the new, classic Craftsman house at 52 Nace. One of the oldest houses on Nace is the “Gibson House” at 46 Nace. Before the Gibsons, the owner was the dairy man Fenton. In 2024 this house was the winner of the City’s Excellence in Integrated Garage Design and the walkers took a group photo in front of its good-looking garage. The walkers went to Howard Ave, to see the disputed 210 address site. There is no home, only a curb cut with a narrow driveway up the hill. The group assumed the site for the proposed condominiums is up there, and it seemed understandable the neighbors have issues. The group went back to Lake and were soon at Beach School’s main entrance. Egbert Beach Elementary can tie its history back to the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. On that April 18th morning, thousands of people fled San Francisco for the East Bay, and Piedmont grew ten times over the next year. Piedmont was incorporated in 1907 and City leaders decided to build two schools to serve the growing community. The “Bonita Avenue School,” later renamed after its land donor, Frank C. Havens, opened in 1911. The “Lake Avenue School” was built in 1913 and renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in 1917 to honor of the first Piedmonter and first Californian officer killed during World War I.
