articles.text: Dear Jim: I had a French Drain and downspout system put in by a reputable drainage contractor about 5 years ago, which worked perfectly fine until last week’s atmospheric river event. About an hour into the deluge, I started to have water come in through my basement floor- something I had never seen before. Now that these heavy rains are becoming more frequent, I’m worried that this problem might get worse over time. Is there anything I can do to make sure my home stays dry for the long haul? –Seth Piedmont The good news is that most of the systems we have installed over the last 30 years have performed extremely well, even in these deluges. However, we’re hearing from other contractors who have had serious issues with their installed work, and homeowners experiencing drainage failures they never expected. So, what’s going wrong, and how can we prevent it? Here is a summary of what we have been observing and the improvements we’ve been implementing to add additional security for our clients. The water-based backup pump is our secret weapon. Drainage systems need to handle more water than ever Recent extreme storms are pushing drainage systems beyond their limits, overwhelming capacity and allowing water to seep into homes in unexpected ways. We’ve seen cases where excess water backs up under floors, overflows through area drains and entry landings, and causes poorly percolating drain fields to fail. To combat this, larger drainage pipes with dual exit points can improve flow, while additional sump pumps at key low points— such as basement entry doors on downslope homes—can provide an extra layer of protection if the primary system is overwhelmed. Overflow protection is essential to prevent backups and ensure long-term drainage reliability. Growing up in Oakland, Tuan began his musical journey in Piedmont’s choirs as a young chorister at the age of six, after a teacher recommended that he join the choir. The Artistic Director of the choir at the time, Bob Geary, would become one of Tuan’s mentors after noticing his talent. “I think at the age of about 10, I called his parents because I wanted to get a feeling for whether they understood how special he was,” said Geary. “And that was the point at which I realized of all the many, many students we’ve had – and many of them have gone on to marvelous lives and careers, both in the arts and in other disciplines – that Eric was one of the very, very few who was the most gifted.” Tuan spent 10 years singing with PEBCC before pursuing higher education. He received a B.A. in Music with Honors from Stanford University and a Master of Music in Choral Studies with Distinction from the University of Cambridge in England, which he obtained with the support of a Gates Cambridge Scholarship. Returning after college, Tuan joined PEBCC faculty in 2015 as conductor of the high school age Ecco group and as composer-in-residence before beginning his tenure as Artistic Director in July 2019. Tuan’s current choral training program serves more than 350 youth singers and leads its top ensembles in concerts throughout the world. Tuan’s dedication to musical exploration has led him to write more than 30 works, with compositions being performed by Luther College Collegiate Chorale, Lux, Vino Ensemble, Volti, and others. Tuan’s musical catalogue shows a long history of works displaying wisdom, social justice, and spirituality, such as his 2023 works “Vision in the Coast Range” and “Let Them Not Say.” “I really like telling stories that bring humanity into some of the more contentious social issues that we face now,” said Tuan in an interview with the Post. “I feel like the world is so polarized and that people and issues can become very abstract. I’m interested in my music telling individual stories very deeply so that people can feel the human connection and experience.” Choral music, undoubtedly beautiful for the audience, seems to give its greatest treasures to its singers and musicians. Tuan spoke at length about the deep connections of choir music as an art form. “I think singing together is a deeply primal thing,” said Tuan. “I think it’s one of these things that make us human. Singing together – I mean, it literally synchronizes your body and your breath and your heart because you’re all breathing together. So there’s this wonderful feeling of connection.” Youth choir and community For Tuan, singing is more than just sound – it’s community. For students in the program, singing together allows them to make friends across a wide range of people and cultures. “Our singers often say that it’s a safe place for them. It’s a place where they’ve made their deepest friends and cherished lifelong experiences,” said Tuan. “The level of musical training that they receive and the opportunities that affords is huge.” The program is also centered around student growth, with a number of programs designed to support youth engagement and youth leadership. The leadership team, elected by the choir, is in charge of creating choir sweatshirts, tour T-shirts, and even sending weekly emails. PEBCC also has a teaching assistant program, where high school aged singers go back into their elementary choir classrooms and assist with teaching. This is often the first job for many singers in this program. When asked if he had any advice for young people looking to pursue their passions, Tuan encouraged youth to look for new experiences. “Don’t be afraid to take risks because often every experience, whether it’s positive or negative, teaches you something,” said Tuan. “Don’t be afraid to make mistakes. Don’t be afraid to try new things… Nourish yourself as a person, because that feeds into your art.” Echoes of Eureka Of all his works to this point, Tuan is most proud of his opera, Echoes of Eureka. “I took a lot of risks in writing it. And I’ve really enjoyed reaching out to and collaborating with community members in Humboldt County and the API community there and historians who have been really generous in sharing their work with me to create this piece,” said Tuan. Echoes of Eureka promises to be a moving opera with a message that is especially relevant in the current American landscape. “It’s almost therapeutic to be rehearsing it right now because the story it tells is so relevant,” said Tuan. “It reminds me both of the contemporary challenges we face and also of the really powerful resistance for civil rights that these Chinese immigrants showed in the 1880s and 1890s. I hope that it allows us both to learn from and be inspired by the past right now.” Echoes of Eureka will premiere as a part of PEBCC’s Making History Concert on April 12, as well as being performed at a music festival in Eureka on May 2-4. Piedmont Real Estate Update February 2025 The Less Glamorous Aspects of Home Ownership With heavy rains and atmospheric storms hitting the East Bay, homeowners face flooding, sewer backups, and pest infestations. While rain is beneficial, it can also expose vulnerabilities in your home. Taking action now can help avoid costly repairs. Preventing Sewer Backups Atmospheric storms can overwhelm East Bay sewer systems, leading to backups. Reduce the risk by: Inspecting Your Sewer Lateral – Many homes have aging pipes with cracks or root intrusion. A professional camera inspection can detect problems early. A number of East Bay plumbers will run this inspection for free. Call us for a referral. Protecting Against Tree Roots – Tree roots can infiltrate pipes, causing blockages. Consider a root barrier or replacing old pipes with root-resistant materials. Reducing Water Use During Storms – Limiting laundry and dishwasher use can ease strain on the system. Installing a Backwater Valve – This prevents sewage from backing up into your home during heavy storms. Water Weeps & Drainage Water weeps (drainage spaces in stucco and windows) prevent trapped moisture from building up. However, blocked weeps or poor drainage can lead to mold, leaks, and foundation issues. Check & Clear Weep Holes – Ensure they’re not clogged with dirt, paint, or debris. Improve Drainage – Redirect downspouts at least 5' from your foundation. If water pools, consider a French drain or sump pump. Inspect Doors & Windows – Leaky seals allow rain to seep in. Reapply caulking and weatherstripping as needed. Rodent-Proofing Your Home Colder temperatures and rain drive rodents indoors, especially in neighborhoods near open fields, creeks, and wooded areas. Prevent infestations by: Sealing Entry Points – Close gaps around vents, pipes, and foundation cracks with steel wool or caulking. Mice can squeeze through holes as small as a dime! Cleaning Gutters & Trimming Trees – Clogged gutters and overgrown branches provide shelter and easy access for pests/rodents. Eliminating Food Sources – Store food in airtight containers, secure pet food, and rodent-proof compost bins. Checking Crawl Spaces & Attics – Look for droppings or gnawed materials. If you suspect an infestation, act quickly. You can hire a rodent company to assist you.
